final:
Everyone assumes fast food got expensive for the same reason everything else did: inflation, supply chains, wages going up across the board. But a fast-food combo meal rose more than 100% between 2014 and 2024, outpacing gasoline, movie tickets, and median hourly wages over the same period. Wages and inflation together don't account for all of it.

So where did the rest of the increase actually come from?

You pull into the drive-through, order the same combo you've been ordering for years, and the total comes back almost twelve dollars. Not at a sit-down restaurant. Not with a drink upgrade or a side you didn't ask for. Just the burger, the fries, the soda — the thing that was supposed to be fast and cheap and available to everyone.

In 2014, a McDonald's Quarter Pounder with Cheese meal cost $5.39. By 2024, that same meal was running $11.99. Visual Capitalist tracked the average price movement across ten major fast-food restaurants from 2014 to 2024 and found a 63% average increase, with McDonald's up 100%. Those aren't outliers.

The thing that was supposed to sit below the threshold of a real financial decision quietly became one of the faster-rising prices in the consumer basket, without a single announcement, without a moment anyone pointed to and said: this is when it changed.

The standard explanation, that costs went up so prices went up, turns out to account for only part of what happened. The rest needs a harder look.

The industry has an answer ready, and it is not wrong — it is just incomplete.

Start with what the numbers actually show. According to the National Restaurant Association, food and labor costs for the average restaurant each rose 35% over the last five years. Those two lines move together, and combined they consume a substantial share of every dollar a quick-service operator brings in — roughly 30% each for labor and food, by National Restaurant Association benchmarking, before you add occupancy and everything else. When your two biggest cost lines each climb sharply in five years, raising prices is not a choice so much as arithmetic.

The commodity side of that pressure was real and sharp. Beef, chicken, and cooking-oil costs each peaked at double-digit percentage increases from their 2020 baselines during the 2021–2023 run-up. A survey covering that period found restaurant costs overall rose 11.7% in a single year, with the largest documented increases coming from raw materials and labor simultaneously, two cost lines moving hard in the same direction at the same time. By April 2022, fast-food menu prices were already up 7.0% year over year, according to BLS data cited by Restaurant Business Online. Then, in the twelve months ending February 2023, the BLS category for limited-service meals and snacks rose 7.2%, one of the fastest rates in the series and a key turning point in fast-food affordability.

By the time that 7.2% landed, the cumulative toll from 2019 to 2023 had reached roughly 28% for limited-service meals, compared to about 24% for full-service restaurants over the same stretch.

So the trade press ran the story, and it was accurate as far as it went: inputs spiked, menus followed. Analysts cited labor. Analysts cited beef. The explanation landed because it was grounded in real data that any operator could point to on their own books.

But the National Restaurant Association's own figures quietly complicate the story they tell. Food costs up 35%. Labor costs up 35%. Average menu prices up 31% between February 2020 and April 2025, less than either input cost line. If prices were simply chasing costs, you would expect the menu line to meet or exceed the cost lines, not trail them.

What the commodity story cannot carry, though, is what came after the peak. Menu prices kept climbing even as overall inflation moderated.

What happened to the portion on the other side of that price was quieter, and in some ways more consequential.

When input costs spiked, operators faced a choice that the industry's 3-to-5% profit margin made brutally simple. That margin, documented by NACS, leaves almost no room for a cost shock to land without a response. So two levers got pulled at once: prices went up on the menu board, and the amount of food on the plate quietly came down. One move is visible. The other one barely registers until you're halfway through a burger that used to last longer.

That second lever is shrinkflation, and it ran alongside the price increases, not instead of them. A report documented the practice directly: higher food costs led restaurants to shrink portions on some menu items while simultaneously raising prices. The result is a compounding effect that a standard price index is not built to catch. The BLS's CPI for limited-service meals captures what you pay, not what you get for it — the agency's own methodology helps capture some non-portion price changes but not every shrinkflation adjustment. So when the CPI for limited-service meals and snacks rose 3.2% over the twelve months ending February 2026, that number describes the price movement on the menu board. Nothing about whether the sandwich got smaller.

Thirty-five percent of QSR customers told the Harris Poll they had noticed shrinkflation at quick-service restaurants over the prior year. That's not a majority, but it's also not a rounding error: more than one in three customers noticed the portion shift.

Eighty-two percent of operators raised menu prices in 2023, according to a 2026 restaurant inflation analysis, and 61% planned to do it again in 2024. A 2024 analysis cited by the Louisiana Restaurant Association framed the target: operators were trying to preserve roughly a 5% margin as costs moved hard against them.

Margin defense is a real and legitimate business pressure. But it also means price increases were not simply tracking costs — they were calibrated to protect a return. And when portions shrank at the same time prices rose, the real unit cost to the consumer moved further than either number alone suggests.

So take the labor cost story at face value for a moment and follow it all the way through the arithmetic. Labor runs about 30% of a quick-service operator's costs, and in one restaurant sample, minimum-wage costs came to just 4% to 10% of total costs. That distinction matters, because rising labor costs and minimum-wage hikes driving prices up are not the same claim.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago put a number on the actual price response: for every 1% increase in the minimum wage, fast-food restaurant prices rise about 0.139%. A separate study of fast-food chains found that a one-dollar increase in the minimum wage raised average menu prices by approximately seven cents.

Put those figures next to the actual price movement and a gap opens immediately. Limited-service meal prices climbed 26% from 2019 to 2024. The minimum wage increases that happened across that period were real, but running them through the empirical pass-through rates the literature documents, mandated wage costs alone cannot produce that number. The arithmetic does not close.

The cost-pass-through research on broader labor expenses tells a similar story. A 2026 Berkeley IRLE paper, examining the effects of a twenty-dollar minimum wage, estimated that consumers absorbed about 50% of the higher labor costs through prices — not all of it, roughly half. So even when you expand the lens beyond mandated minimums to total labor cost pressure, the evidence points consistently toward partial transmission, not full recovery through the menu.

What that means structurally: if labor and food costs each rose roughly 35% and operators pass through only around half of those increases, the cost-driven explanation accounts for a meaningful portion of the price rise, but not all of it. Another lever was available, and the data show it got pulled.

The Harris Poll asked people what a fair price for a full quick-service meal looks like. Forty-seven percent said five to nine dollars and ninety-nine cents, essentially the five-to-ten-dollar range. And by 2024, some individual items at major chains had more than doubled in price from a decade earlier.

The consequence was not abstract. Eighty-one percent of adults who order from quick-service restaurants at least once a year told the Harris Poll that prices were higher than a year ago — not higher than a decade ago, higher than last year. And only 32% agreed that quick-service restaurants still offered affordable meal options.

Behavior followed perception. Sixty-two percent of respondents said they were eating less fast food because it cost more. Seventy-five percent said cooking at home was more economical.

The word that crystallized it came from a LendingTree-related survey: 78% of respondents said fast food had become a luxury.

Numerator tracked quick-service restaurant prices from January 2018 through 2026 and found they had climbed 53.9% — against a 33.2% rise in the overall consumer basket over the same stretch. That 20-point spread is not a rounding difference. It is the distance between a category that tracked the economy and one that consistently outran it. The BLS data narrow the window and sharpen the picture further: limited-service meal prices rose about 28% from 2019 to 2023, while overall CPI rose roughly 19% across those same four years. Against the 26% rise in limited-service meal prices from 2019 to 2024, cumulative headline inflation was roughly 21%, and real wage growth was roughly flat.

By May 2026, the National Restaurant Association put the rise in average menu prices since February 2020 at 36%, up from the 31% it reported through April 2025. BLS data put limited-service meal prices 27.2% higher in February 2024 than in February 2020. Both figures describe the same run-up from different vantage points, and together they show a price level that kept moving even as overall inflation moderated.

That is the part the cost story struggles with. Goods costs were up roughly 31% since 2014, and the commodity pressure through the early 2020s was genuine. The Goldman Sachs data make the asymmetry legible: non-manager wages were up 35.9% since January 2017, and fast-food meal prices were up more than 41% over that same period. Wages — an input industry and analysts most often cited alongside food and other operating costs as drivers — rose less than the prices attributed to covering them.

What the data show beyond that is a price level that moved further than costs alone predict, stayed there after the acute pressure faded, and landed on consumers whose wages did not keep pace with the menu board.

Which brings it back to the drive-through. The person pulling up to the window in 2024 was not experiencing an abstraction. They were experiencing the cumulative output of the commodity run-up, the labor cost pressure, the margin target, the shrinking portion, and the pricing that stayed elevated after the shock passed — compressed into a single number on a screen. Twelve dollars. The meal that was supposed to cost less than a decision. The one that, for a decade, you ordered without checking your wallet first. The meal that cost $5.39 in 2014 was running $11.99 by 2024, and 78% of respondents now call fast food a luxury.
